THOUGHT: This 3-year-old child presents with tachypnea (RR 40/min), tachycardia (HR 130 bpm), hepatomegaly (liver enlarged 1.5× normal), bilateral pitting edema, mild abdominal distension, and mild pulmonary rales — all signs of systemic congestion and heart failure. The absence of fever, cough, or respiratory infection symptoms makes primary pulmonary or infectious etiologies less likely. The fixed split S2 on auscultation is a classic physical finding in atrial septal defect (ASD), and the echocardiogram confirms an ASD with left-to-right shunt. In young children, even moderate-sized ASDs can lead to volume overload of the right heart and pulmonary overcirculation; over time — especially if undiagnosed — this may progress to right ventricular volume overload, elevated right-sided pressures, tricuspid regurgitation, and eventually right heart failure manifesting as hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, and ascites (though shifting dullness is absent here, suggesting early or mild fluid retention). The chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly without pulmonary edema — consistent with chronic volume overload rather than acute pulmonary congestion. Normal liver enzymes and albumin argue against primary hepatic disease. CBC is unremarkable, ruling out significant anemia or infection as drivers. The constellation — tachypnea + tachycardia + hepatomegaly + peripheral edema + fixed split S2 + echocardiographic confirmation of ASD with shunt — points to congestive heart failure secondary to chronic left-to-right shunting through an ASD. While ASDs are often asymptomatic in early childhood, symptomatic heart failure can occur by age 2–4 years, particularly with larger defects or comorbidities (none present here). Thus, the most unifying diagnosis is heart failure due to hemodynamically significant ASD.

DIAGNOSIS: Congestive heart failure secondary to atrial septal defect
